title: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
research_question: This paper investigates whether noisy workplaces in low- and middle-income countries impair workers' cognitive functions, reduce productivity, and whether workers are aware of these effects, influencing their willingness to pay for quiet working conditions.

participants.description: Experiment 1: 128 manual laborers. Experiment 2: 213 individuals. All participants were recruited from groups of manual laborers seeking day work at textile factories in Nairobi, Kenya. The sample is demographically similar to many poor communities.
participants.recruitment: Recruited from groups of manual laborers who gather at the gates of nearby textile factories hoping to be hired for a day's work.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Engine noise generated by a car engine (used for automechanic training classes) added to the ambient noise of sewing machines. Control condition noise was equivalent to a home dishwasher; treatment condition noise was equivalent to a home vacuum cleaner. Noise levels did not exceed 80 dB.

measures.instrument: Number of pockets created per session, total points earned (quantity + quality), number of pockets meeting various quality criteria. Transformed using inverse hyperbolic sine.

Index derived from a battery of cognitive tests measuring attention, working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and higher-level reasoning (first factor of common factor analysis of percentage correct and reaction times).
Key presses on a keyboard for ten minutes (alternating A and B keys).

measures.construct: Willingness to Pay (WTP) for quiet working conditions
measures.instrument: Modified Becker, DeGroot, and Marschak (BDM) procedure using a binary search over KSh0–200.

measures.construct: Beliefs about noise impact on productivity
measures.instrument: Respondents distributed ten beans across ten bins of possible scores for future performance in quiet vs. noise under different compensation schemes.
Noise level (A-weighted decibels), CO2 (parts per million), humidity (percent), temperature (Celsius).
Savings/withdrawals from an account, maize flour purchase (inattention), willingness to stay and work an additional hour (effort).

findings.antecedent: Disutility from noise (WTP for quiet in flat-rate condition)
findings.consequent: Productivity losses from noise (estimated within-person treatment effects)
findings.mechanism: Disutility from noise and productivity losses from noise are uncorrelated, suggesting inefficient worker sorting if workers neglect productive impacts.
findings.quote: disutility and productivity losses appear to be unrelated. This suggests that the composition of workers sorting into noisy work environments could be significantly altered by workers neglecting the productive impact of noise.

mechanisms: Impaired cognitive function (attention, working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, higher-level reasoning) due to noise.
Lack of awareness or inattention to the productive impact of noise.
Incorrect or imprecise beliefs about the impact of noise on productivity.
Disutility from noise (annoyance) is distinct from productivity effects.
moderators: Worker ability (median split of control performance)
Time (week of experiment, hour of session)
Typical noise exposure in daily life
Compensation scheme (piece rate vs. flat rate)
Prompting consideration of beliefs before WTP elicitation
implementation_implications: Policymakers should consider noise pollution as a significant environmental pollutant with economic costs.
Governments should collect comprehensive data on noise exposure.
Regulations limiting unnecessary urban noise sources (e.g., car horns) could reduce noise levels without significant efficiency costs.
Raising awareness among workers and firms about the potential effects of noise on productivity could improve outcomes at minimal cost.

limitations: Logistical constraints prevented a sufficiently long sample for a sufficient amount of time to observe full adaptation or learning curves.
Results may be specific to the textile production task and noise combination; extrapolation to other contexts should be done with caution.
Noise levels were kept below 80 dB for ethical reasons, which are lower than typical factory noise, potentially reducing perceived need for abatement.
Productivity is a relatively random outcome, making it difficult for respondents to infer treatment effects over the experiment's duration.
The sample was recruited from a specific population (seeking employment at the same factories, living in the same settlement), limiting the true variance in past noise exposure.
The experiment's learning environment might not fully reflect real-world learning processes.
The study does not assess whether firms are aware of noise effects, screen workers, or optimally abate.

environmental_features: Increased noise level (7 dB increase from dishwasher to vacuum cleaner equivalent)
control_conditions: Baseline noise level (e.g., quiet office environment)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Increased environmental noise increases cognitive load, thereby reducing available cognitive resources for task performance and decreasing productivity.

mechanism_chain.description: Increased noise leads to cognitive distraction and increased mental effort, which depletes cognitive resources necessary for focused task performance, ultimately reducing productivity.

instruments_used.description: Total pockets produced in textile training course
Standardized cognitive tasks (e.g., reaction time, working memory tasks)
